principles: The digest must honor the contract its own doc comment states: collapse incidental differences, preserve substantive ones.
Narrow each over-broad normalization rule rather than deleting it, so the breaker keeps catching genuine repeats.
Prove both directions in the same test matrix, because a one-directional fix can silently disable the breaker.
Change nothing outside the digest function: threshold, counters, assessBreaker, reset semantics and the recovery flow stay exactly as they are.
Assert the counter consequence, not just the hash, because the operator-visible failure is a frozen story rather than a string mismatch.
drivers: A false freeze costs an interactive human TTY acknowledgement, which is the most expensive recovery this workflow has.
Loosening the digest too far would let a runaway agent regain an unbounded retry loop, so the fix must not simply make every reason unique.
The remaining stories of this program must pass the same gates that trigger the false freeze, so the fix has to land before them.

options.name: Narrow the normalizer and drop the truncation
pros: Fixes all four reproduced collapse classes in one function.
Keeps every incidental-token rule that makes the breaker useful, only scoping each to what it was meant to match.
Testable in both directions from one smoke matrix with per-rule revert proofs.
No call site, no artifact schema and no stored counter format changes.
cons: The normalizer stays a set of text rules, so a future rejection message with an unanticipated volatile token could still over-distinguish.
Removing the truncation means the hash input is unbounded unless a sanity bound is retained.

options.name: Digest a structured failure code instead of the message text
pros: Immune to message wording entirely; two failures are the same exactly when their codes match.
Would also make the counter file human-readable.
cons: Requires every rejection site across the CLI to emit a structured code first, which is a far larger change than the defect warrants.
The bump call site at cli-engine.ts:1508 receives only an Error message, so the plumbing would have to change too.
Leaves the defect live for as long as that migration takes, blocking the remaining program stories.

options.name: Raise the truncation bound only
pros: Fixes the dominant class, since the DEV-gate header collapse is caused by the bound.
cons: Leaves the phase-pair, checklist-ordinal and file-path collapses untouched, so false freezes continue from those.
Picks a new magic number with no principled value, inviting the same defect at a larger size.

chosen: Narrow the normalizer and drop the truncation
rationale: The reproduced defect has four causes and only this option addresses all of them while leaving the breaker's protective behavior intact. The structured-code option is the better long-term shape but is disproportionate to a defect isolated in one pure function, and it would block the remaining program stories behind a cross-cutting migration. Raising the bound alone is rejected because three of the four reproduced collapse classes are caused by the token rules, not the bound.

preMortem.scenario: The narrowed normalizer distinguishes so much that the breaker never fires again.
preMortem.trigger: A retried command emits a reason carrying a volatile token that no remaining rule normalizes, for example an elapsed-time figure or a pid.
preMortem.consequence: A genuinely stuck agent retries indefinitely and the convergence breaker, the mechanism meant to stop exactly that, silently never trips.
preMortem.mitigation: CHK-004 requires must-still-collapse cases that drive bumpGateFailureCount twice and assert maxGateFailureCount reaches 2 and assessBreaker trips, so the protective direction is proven, not assumed. The rules that absorb timestamps, hex ids, machine paths and free-standing counters are all retained.

preMortem.scenario: The truncation is removed and an enormous reason string makes digest computation pathological.
preMortem.trigger: A gate failure carries an entire validation transcript or a stack trace as its message.
preMortem.consequence: Every failed command pays an unbounded hashing cost, degrading an already slow lifecycle command.
preMortem.mitigation: Retain a large sanity bound far above any realistic rejection message instead of removing the bound outright, and cover it with an explicit edge-lane check so the bound's existence is proven rather than assumed.

preMortem.scenario: The fix passes its own smoke but the real gate rejection still collapses.
preMortem.trigger: The smoke uses short synthetic fixtures, exactly the weakness of the existing guard at convergence-breaker-smoke.ts:180-182, so it never reproduces the real message shape.
preMortem.consequence: The story lands, the operator hits the same false freeze on the next story, and the defect is now believed fixed.
preMortem.mitigation: The matrix reconstructs the real DEV-gate rejection render from machine.ts:179 and renderProofStoryDiagnosticReport with gap texts quoted from proofstory.ts, and the standing RED harness reproduces the same digests independently before and after the change.

preMortem.scenario: Existing stories carry accumulated counter entries keyed by the old digest.
preMortem.trigger: A story that already has gate-failure-counts.json entries hits a new failure after the change, and the new key does not match the stored one.
preMortem.consequence: Previously accumulated counts appear to reset, so a story that was one failure away from tripping starts over.
preMortem.mitigation: Accept this deliberately: the stored counts are per-story ephemeral progress signals that resetGateFailureCounts already clears on every successful mutation, and a reset that loses a stale count is strictly safer than a false freeze. Record it as a known effect rather than adding a migration.
